old <- options(width = 100L)

The [comparison with targets](v07-vs-targets.html) lists several features
that {targets} has and {pipeflow} does not: file tracking, metadata,
runs in a fresh R process, and more. Many of them can be emulated with
existing {pipeflow} functions and a few lines of your own code. This
article shows one recipe per feature. Each section names the {targets}
feature, shows the recipe as running code, and says where the emulation
stops.

```{r load-package}
library(pipeflow)
```

## File targets {#file-targets}

In {targets}, a target with `format = "file"` tracks a file: when the file
changes, the target and everything downstream of it run again.

{pipeflow} doesn't look at files. But it does notice when a parameter
changes. So give the step that reads the file an extra parameter, here
`rev`, that it ignores, and set it to a fingerprint of the file before
each run.

```{r file-pipeline}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(data.frame(x = 1:3), path, row.names = FALSE)

p <- pip_new("files") |>
    pip_add("read", \(path, rev = NULL) read.csv(path),
        params = list(path = path)
    ) |>
    pip_add("total", \(data = ~read) sum(data$x))

refresh <- function(p) {
    pip_set_params(p, list(rev = unname(tools::md5sum(path))))
}
```

The first run computes everything.

```{r file-first-run}
refresh(p)
p
pip_run(p)
```

Setting a parameter to the value it already has is not a change (see
[Setting Identical Values](v01-get-started.html#setting-identical-values)).
So if the file is unchanged, `refresh()` leaves the states alone and
nothing runs.

```{r file-unchanged}
refresh(p)
p
pip_run(p)
```

Once the file is edited, its fingerprint changes. `refresh()` outdates the
step that reads it and all steps downstream of it.

```{r file-edited}
write.csv(data.frame(x = 1:4), path, row.names = FALSE)

refresh(p)
p
pip_run(p)
p[["total", "out"]]
```

To refresh and run in one go, use `refresh(p) |> pip_run()`.

**Variants.** `file.mtime()` and `file.size()` are cheaper than
`tools::md5sum()`, because they don't read the file. They are also less
reliable: a copy or a `git checkout` changes the modification time without
changing the content, and an edit can keep the size. For several files,
`tools::md5sum(c(path1, path2))` returns one hash per file, and any change
in the vector outdates the step. If different steps read different files,
give each its own parameter (`raw_rev`, `lookup_rev`, ...).

**Limits.**

* The fingerprint is only as fresh as the last `refresh()`. Forget to call
  it, and an edited file goes unnoticed.
* Only files that steps read are covered. {targets} also notices when a
  file that a target wrote was changed or deleted. Here you have to rerun
  that step yourself.

## Rebuild when code changes {#code-changes}

{targets} reruns a target when its command or a function it calls changes,
including your own helper functions.

In {pipeflow}, replacing a step function with `pip_replace()` already
outdates the step and its downstream steps. What {pipeflow} can't see is a
helper function that the step calls. Use the same trick as for files, with
a hash of the helper as fingerprint.

```{r code-pipeline}
clean <- function(x) round(x, 1)

p <- pip_new("code") |>
    pip_add("data", \(n = 4) seq_len(n) / 3) |>
    pip_add("cleaned", \(x = ~data, code = NULL) clean(x))

refresh_code <- function(p) {
    pip_set_params(p, list(code = rlang::hash(utils::removeSource(clean))))
}

refresh_code(p) |> pip_run(lgr = NULL)
p
```

`removeSource()` matters: in an interactive session, R keeps the source
code of every function you define, and the hash would cover it. Then
running the same definition again would change the hash. Without the
source, defining the same helper again changes nothing:

```{r code-unchanged}
clean <- function(x) round(x, 1)

refresh_code(p)
p
```

A new version of the helper outdates the step that calls it.

```{r code-changed}
clean <- function(x) round(x, 2)

refresh_code(p)
p
pip_run(p)
p[["cleaned", "out"]]
```

**Limits.**

* You list the helpers yourself. {targets} finds the functions a target
  calls, and the functions those call, by static code analysis. Here, a
  helper of a helper is only covered if you add it to the hash, e.g.
  `rlang::hash(lapply(list(clean, other), utils::removeSource))`.
* Like {targets}, this does not track functions from packages. A package
  update does not outdate anything.

## A metadata table like `tar_meta()` {#metadata}

`tar_meta()` returns a table with one row per target: when it ran, how long
it took, the size of its output and the error if it failed.

The step table of a pipeline (`pip_data()`) has most of this. `time_start`
is the start of the step's last run. `time` is the end of its last
*successful* run, so a failed step keeps the `time` of an earlier
success (or `NA`). The duration is `time - time_start`, but only for
steps that did not fail. The output of a failed step is the condition that
it signalled.

```{r meta-function}
meta <- function(p) {
    d <- as.data.frame(pip_data(p))
    ok <- d$state != "failed"
    seconds <- as.numeric(difftime(d$time, d$time_start, units = "secs"))
    bytes <- vapply(d$out, \(x) as.numeric(object.size(x)), numeric(1))
    error <- vapply(
        d$out,
        \(x) if (inherits(x, "error")) conditionMessage(x) else NA_character_,
        character(1)
    )
    data.frame(
        step = d$step,
        state = d$state,
        start = d$time_start,
        seconds = ifelse(ok, round(seconds, 2), NA),
        bytes = ifelse(ok, bytes, NA),
        error = error
    )
}
```

Let's use it on a pipeline with a slow first step and a step that fails
for large inputs.

```{r meta-pipeline}
p <- pip_new("meta") |>
    pip_add("load", \(n = 3) {
        Sys.sleep(0.2)
        seq_len(n)
    }) |>
    pip_add("fit", \(x = ~load) {
        if (length(x) > 3) stop("too many values")
        sum(x)
    }) |>
    pip_add("report", \(x = ~fit) paste("total:", x))

pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
meta(p)
```

Now the input grows and `fit` fails. With `on_error = "continue"`, the run
goes on, and `report` is skipped because its input failed.

```{r meta-failed}
pip_set_params(p, list(n = 5))
pip_run(p, lgr = NULL, on_error = "continue")
meta(p)
```

The table shows the error of `fit`. `report` is `outdated` and still has
the start time and output of the first run.

**Limits.**

* Only the last run of each step is recorded. Keep a history by appending
  `meta(p)` to a table after each run.
* Warnings are not recorded, and there is no hash of the output.

## Metadata stored with each output {#output-metadata}

{targets} stores metadata such as size and format along with each target.

In {pipeflow}, the generic `pip_output_value()` is called on every output
right after its step returns. A method for your own class can attach the
metadata to the output itself. See
[Annotated step outputs](v05e-output-value.html) for the details.

```{r output-metadata}
tracked <- function(x) structure(x, class = c("tracked", class(x)))

pip_output_value.tracked <- function(x, ctx = list(), ...) {
    attr(x, "meta") <- list(
        step = ctx[["step"]],
        time = ctx[["time"]],
        class = setdiff(class(x), "tracked"),
        bytes = as.numeric(object.size(x))
    )
    x
}
registerS3method("pip_output_value", "tracked", pip_output_value.tracked)

p <- pip_new("tracked") |>
    pip_add("cars", \(n = 5) tracked(head(mtcars, n)))

pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
str(attr(p[["cars", "out"]], "meta"))
```

**Limits.** Each step has to mark its output with the class. Methods are
meant for your own classes, not for base classes such as `data.frame`.

## Reproducible random numbers {#seeds}

{targets} gives each target its own seed (see `tar_seed()`), so a target
draws the same random numbers no matter which other targets run.

In {pipeflow}, steps draw from the global random number stream. Steps that
are skipped don't draw, so the numbers a step gets depend on which steps
ran before it. Here, `b` gets different numbers when it reruns alone than
in a full run, although the seed is the same.

```{r seed-problem}
p <- pip_new("rng") |>
    pip_add("a", \(n = 3) rnorm(n)) |>
    pip_add("b", \(n = 3, scale = 1) scale * rnorm(n))

set.seed(1)
pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
b_full <- p[["b", "out"]]

pip_set_params(p, list(scale = 2))
set.seed(1)
pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
p[["b", "out"]]
2 * b_full
```

The recipe: give each step its own seed parameter (`seed_a`, `seed_b`, ...)
and set it inside the step. Use different names, because params with the
same name share one value: `pip_add()` warns if they differ, and
`pip_set_params()` sets them all at once.
A small helper also restores the global random number state afterwards, so
running the pipeline doesn't change the numbers that the rest of your
session draws. `withr::with_seed()` does the same, if you have {withr}
installed.

```{r seed-helper}
with_seed <- function(seed, code) {
    old <- get0(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv(), inherits = FALSE)
    on.exit(
        if (is.null(old)) {
            rm(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv())
        } else {
            assign(".Random.seed", old, envir = globalenv())
        }
    )
    set.seed(seed)
    code
}
```

Now `b` gets the same numbers, whether it runs alone or with `a`.

```{r seed-recipe}
p <- pip_new("rng") |>
    pip_add("a", \(n = 3, seed_a = 1) with_seed(seed_a, rnorm(n))) |>
    pip_add("b", \(n = 3, scale = 1, seed_b = 2) {
        with_seed(seed_b, scale * rnorm(n))
    })

pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
b_full <- p[["b", "out"]]

pip_set_params(p, list(scale = 2))
pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
p[["b", "out"]]
2 * b_full
```

**Limits.**

* You choose the seeds. {targets} derives them from the target names.
* Each step needs its own seed parameter name. A shared `seed` would get
  one value in all steps, so they would all draw the same numbers.
* Steps that run code in parallel need a parallel-safe generator, as with
  any R code.

## Results that survive an R restart {#persistence}

{targets} stores every target on disk, so the results survive when R is
restarted.

A {pipeflow} pipeline is an R object. Save it with `saveRDS()` after
running it, and read it back with `readRDS()` in a new session. The
functions, parameters, outputs and states are all kept. The dependency
graph lives in C++ and can't be saved directly. It is rebuilt
automatically the first time the pipeline is used. Let's save the file
pipeline from [above](#file-targets).

```{r persist-save}
p <- pip_new("files") |>
    pip_add("read", \(path, rev = NULL) read.csv(path),
        params = list(path = path)
    ) |>
    pip_add("total", \(data = ~read) sum(data$x))

refresh(p) |> pip_run(lgr = NULL)

file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(p, file)
rm(p)
```

Here, `rm()` stands in for the restart. After `readRDS()`, the steps are
still `done`. The fingerprint of the file was saved too, so `refresh()` only
reruns steps if the file changed in the meantime.

```{r persist-restore}
p <- readRDS(file)
p

refresh(p) |> pip_run()
```

Step functions keep their enclosing environment. If a step function was
created inside another function, that environment is saved with it,
including every object in it, which can make the file large. The global
environment is never saved: helpers such as `refresh()` or `with_seed()`
have to be defined again in the new session.

**Limits.**

* Nothing is saved automatically. If R crashes during a run, the results of
  that run are lost. {targets} saves each target as soon as it is built.
* The whole pipeline is one file, written and read as a whole, and it must
  fit in memory.

## Running in a fresh R process {#fresh-process}

`tar_make()` runs the pipeline in a new R process by default. The results
then can't depend on objects that happen to be lying around in your
session.

With [{callr}](https://callr.r-lib.org), you can run a {pipeflow} pipeline
in a new R process as well. The pipeline is copied to the new process,
run there and copied back.

```{r fresh-function}
run_fresh <- function(p, ...) {
    callr::r(
        function(p, ...) {
            library(pipeflow)
            pip_run(p, ...)
            p
        },
        args = list(p, ...)
    )
}

p <- pip_new("fresh") |>
    pip_add("data", \(n = 5) seq_len(n)) |>
    pip_add("total", \(x = ~data) sum(x))

p <- run_fresh(p, lgr = NULL)
p
```

What you get back is a new pipeline object, so assign it (`p <-`). Views
and other references to the old object don't see the results.

This is also where you find out what a step needs from your session. A
step that calls a function from a package you attached with `library()`
fails in the new process, where the package is not attached.

```{r fresh-package}
library(tools)

p <- pip_new("fresh") |>
    pip_add("ext", \(path = "data.csv") file_ext(path))

res <- tryCatch(run_fresh(p, lgr = NULL), error = identity)
conditionMessage(res$parent)
```

The same holds for objects and helper functions that a step finds in the
global environment of your session. Use `tools::file_ext()`, or put the
`library()` and `source()` calls that the steps need into the function
that `run_fresh()` runs in the new process.

**Limits.**

* {callr} is not a dependency of {pipeflow}, so you need to install it.
* The whole pipeline, with all outputs, is copied to the new process and
  back on every run. For large outputs, this takes time.
* Starting a new R process takes a moment too, which you pay on every run.

## Which steps are outdated? {#outdated}

`tar_outdated()` lists the targets that the next `tar_make()` would run.

In {pipeflow}, the state of a step tells whether it will run: `new`,
`outdated` and `failed` steps run, `done` steps are skipped. So a view
of these states lists what the next run does.

```{r outdated-view}
p <- pip_new("outdated") |>
    pip_add("a", \(x = 1) x) |>
    pip_add("b", \(a = ~a) a + 1) |>
    pip_add("c", \(b = ~b) b + 1) |>
    pip_add("d", \(y = 1) y)

pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
pip_set_params(p, list(y = 2))
pip_view(p, state = c("new", "outdated", "failed"))
```

The view misses a `done` step that reruns because a step upstream of it
runs. {pipeflow} functions such as `pip_set_params()` or `pip_reset()`
outdate the downstream steps, so this only happens if you set a state by
hand, which outdates no other step (see `?Extract.pipeflow`). Here, `b` and
`c` stay `done`, but they run again with the new output of `a`.

```{r outdated-missed}
p[["a", "state"]] <- "outdated"
pip_view(p, state = c("new", "outdated", "failed"))
pip_run(p)
```

**Limits.**

* Locked steps are listed but skipped. Leave them out with
  `p[state %in% c("new", "outdated", "failed") & !locked]`.
* The states only know about changes made through {pipeflow}. Call
  `refresh()` from the recipes [above](#file-targets) first, so that
  changed files and helpers count.

## What can't be emulated {#cannot-emulate}

Some features of {targets} need infrastructure that {pipeflow} doesn't
have, and a few lines of code won't change that.

* **Distributed workers.** {targets} sends targets to parallel workers,
  also on clusters and in the cloud, via {crew}. {pipeflow} runs the steps
  one after another in one R session. A step can parallelize its own work,
  but the pipeline does not schedule steps on workers.
* **Cloud storage.** {targets} can store targets in AWS S3 or Google Cloud
  Storage. You can upload the file from `saveRDS()` yourself, but there is
  no storage per step.
* **Data larger than RAM.** {targets} keeps each target on disk and loads
  only what a target needs. A {pipeflow} pipeline keeps all outputs in
  memory. A step can return a file path instead of the data, but then you
  manage the files yourself.

If you need these, use {targets}. If you mainly work in an interactive
session or a Shiny app, the recipes above cover a good part of the rest.

```{r restore, include = FALSE}
options(old)
```
